web_title: 2. What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples
book_title: Chapter 2: Inside the $46.4 Billion Machine — Segments, Categories & Real-World Economics
question: Where does Nike actually make its revenue and operating profit today across geographies, brands, and product categories, and which profit engines are subsidizing the turnaround?

epigraph.quote: A brand as large as Nike cannot be managed as a single lifestyle monolith; it is a portfolio of distinct regional P&Ls and sport offenses moving at very different speeds.
epigraph.author: Chapter 2 Forensic Synthesis

web_blocks.html: NIKE, Inc. reports results across four NIKE Brand geographic segments: North America, Europe, Middle East & Africa (EMEA), Greater China, and Asia Pacific & Latin America (APLA) [1, 9]. Results also include Global Brand Divisions (unallocated design, R&D, and global marketing), Converse, and Corporate unallocated expenses [1, 9]. In FY2026 (ended May 31, 2026), consolidated revenue totaled $46,398 million, flat versus $46,309 million in FY2025 [1, 2]. Total NIKE Brand generated $45,202 million (97.4% of consolidated revenue) and $5,855 million in segment EBIT [1, 2]. Converse added $1,174 million (2.5% of revenue) and $18 million in EBIT. That $18 million included a $21 million one-time IEEPA tariff recovery benefit, implying a slight underlying operating loss [1, 2].

By product category, Footwear remains the clear core, driving roughly 66% of total revenue (~$30.5 billion+) [1, 3]. Apparel contributes about 28% (~$13.1 billion+), while Equipment & Accessories accounts for roughly 6% (~$2.8 billion+) [1, 3]. Within the NIKE Brand, Jordan Brand operates as a multi-billion-dollar franchise embedded across all geographic segments. In FY2026, wholesale channels ($27,515 million, ~59% of consolidated sales) regained share over NIKE Direct ($17,692 million, ~38% of sales) as management re-engaged multi-brand retailers [2, 4].

web_blocks.caption: NIKE, Inc. Segment Revenue & EBIT Breakdown (FY2025 vs. FY2026, $ Millions)
web_blocks.takeaway: *FY26 North America EBIT includes a $965M IEEPA tariff recovery benefit (underlying NA EBIT ~$4,411M, or 21.5% margin) and Converse EBIT includes a $21M recovery benefit (underlying -$3M). Ex-recovery, consolidated EBIT was ~$2,864M [1, 2].

web_blocks.html: Regional divergence widened further in Q1 FY2027 (ended August 31, 2026). Consolidated revenue slipped 4% reported (-5% currency-neutral) to $11.2 billion [3]. North America grew 2% to $5.13 billion on a 9% wholesale rebound, while EMEA fell 5% currency-neutral to $3.18 billion [3, 21]. APLA stayed roughly flat, Converse plunged 28% to $263 million, and Greater China dropped 22% reported (-26% currency-neutral) to $1.18 billion [3, 21]. Understanding Nike today requires looking past consolidated averages to see five distinct businesses under one roof.

web_blocks.title: 2.2 Concrete End-to-End Real-World Examples by Major Segment

web_blocks.html: North America (44.2% of FY26 Revenue | Performance Running & Wholesale Rebound): Consider a suburban marathoner in Chicago buying a pair of Nike Pegasus 41 or Vomero 18 daily trainers at Dick's Sporting Goods or a local run-specialty shop for $140 to $160 [19]. She buys the shoe for dual-density ReactX and ZoomX foam cushioning engineered at Nike's Beaverton Sport Research Lab and proven by track athletes. A contract factory in Vietnam (producing 52% of Nike's footwear) builds the shoe for roughly $28 to $35 landed cost [12]. Nike ships it to its Memphis distribution hub, sells it to Dick's at roughly 50% of MSRP (~$75 wholesale), and Dick's retails it at full price [12]. North America wholesale grew 9% in Q1 FY2027 as Nike pruned promotional Classics [3, 21]. That full-price replenishment is the primary engine supporting North America's 21.5% underlying segment margin [3, 21].

EMEA (27.1% of FY26 Revenue | Football & Lifestyle Crossover): Consider a 22-year-old amateur footballer in London or Paris buying Nike Mercurial boots or a Paris Saint-Germain (PSG) match jersey via JD Sports or Nike.com. On-pitch visibility across Premier League and Champions League clubs drives that demand, backed by heavy kit sponsorships inside Global Brand Divisions. Footwear represents roughly 61% of EMEA quarterly revenue ($1,821 million of $2,975 million in Q4 FY26), and apparel contributes 33% ($982 million) [1]. Yet EMEA segment EBIT fell 6% in FY2026 to $2,417 million, and revenue slipped 5% currency-neutral in Q1 FY2027 [1, 3]. Adidas's terrace silhouettes (Samba, Gazelle) alongside On and HOKA captured European urban and running shelf space [14].

Greater China (12.6% of FY26 Revenue | The Former Cash Cow Under Siege): Consider an urban Gen-Z shopper in Shanghai browsing Tmall or a Nike Rise flagship store for running or basketball shoes. Greater China was long Nike's highest-margin growth engine, but revenue dropped from $6,586 million in FY2025 to $5,855 million in FY2026 (-11% reported) [1]. In Q1 FY2027, revenue fell another 22% reported (-26% currency-neutral) to $1.18 billion, after FY2026 EBIT declined 20% to $1,280 million [1, 3, 21]. Domestic rivals led by Anta Sports (RMB 80.2 billion / ~$11.2 billion revenue in 2025) and Li-Ning now match Nike's carbon-plate running tech at 20% to 30% lower prices [17]. Winning local sentiment has forced Nike into heavy discounting on Tmall and in factory outlets [17].

APLA (13.4% of FY26 Revenue | Emerging-Market Footwear & Digital): Consider a young professional in Tokyo, Seoul, or São Paulo buying lifestyle-performance hybrids like the Ava Rover or Jordan retro apparel through local Nike apps or regional distributors. APLA generated $6,234 million in FY2026 revenue (flat YoY) and $1,387 million in segment EBIT (22.2% margin, down 9% YoY) [1]. The region spans mature sneakerhead hubs like Japan and South Korea alongside currency-volatile Latin American and Southeast Asian markets. As a result, its unit economics depend heavily on localized price tiers and foreign-exchange hedging.

Converse (2.5% of FY26 Revenue | Single-Franchise Concentration Risk): Consider a college student buying a $65 Chuck Taylor All Star canvas sneaker at a mall store or outlet. Unlike the NIKE Brand, Converse runs as a standalone unit with minimal technical sport R&D, leaving it exposed to one vulcanized-canvas silhouette. When casual canvas trends cooled, Converse revenue plunged 31% across FY2025–FY2026 from $1,692 million to $1,174 million [1, 2]. Revenue dropped another 28% in Q1 FY2027 to $263 million, wiping out operating profit ($18 million reported EBIT in FY2026, or -$3 million excluding the $21 million tariff recovery) [1, 2, 3].

web_blocks.title: Why Unallocated Costs Matter
paragraphs: Regional segment margins of 19% to 26% look dazzling on paper, but they exclude $4,605 million in Global Brand Divisions costs (global R&D, athlete deals, league sponsorships) and $2,023 million in Corporate overhead [1]. Deducting those $6,628 million of central expenses compressed Nike's FY2026 consolidated EBIT margin to 8.3% reported—and roughly 6.2% excluding the $986 million IEEPA tariff recovery.

book_paragraphs: To read Nike's income statement properly, you and I have to resist the temptation to treat it as one giant sneaker factory. In reality, Nike is five very different regional and brand businesses sitting on top of a massive $6.6 billion central R&D and marketing engine. If you only look at the $46.4 billion top line, you miss the dramatic tug-of-war happening underneath.

Start with North America, which still supplies 44.2% of total revenue—$20.51 billion in FY2026—and $5.38 billion in reported segment EBIT. Now, be a forensic analyst for a second: $965 million of that North America EBIT came from a one-time IEEPA tariff recovery benefit booked in the fourth quarter. Strip that out, and North America earned roughly $4.41 billion, a healthy 21.5% segment margin. Picture how those dollars are actually made: a marathoner walks into Dick's Sporting Goods in Chicago, tries on a $145 Nike Pegasus 41 or Vomero 18 built with ZoomX foam, and pays full price. A Vietnamese contract factory built it for roughly $30, Nike sold it to Dick's at around $75 wholesale, and both sides made money. That full-price wholesale engine is finally humming again, growing 9% in North America in Q1 FY2027.

Now cross the Atlantic to EMEA, your second-largest profit pool at $12.57 billion in FY2026 revenue and $2.42 billion in segment EBIT. Here, the story is a fistfight. A young footballer in London buying Mercurial cleats or a PSG jersey still trusts the Swoosh on the pitch, which keeps footwear at over 60% of EMEA sales. Yet walk down any high street in Paris or Berlin, and Adidas has reclaimed terrace lifestyle mindshare while On and HOKA have carved up specialty running. EMEA's EBIT slipped 6% in FY2026, and revenue fell 5% currency-neutral in Q1 FY2027.

Then there is Greater China, the former crown jewel that has turned into Nike's sharpest headache. Revenue there fell from $6.59 billion in FY2025 to $5.86 billion in FY2026, and then dropped another 22% reported—26% in constant currency—to $1.18 billion in Q1 FY2027. Why? Because an urban runner in Shanghai no longer views Nike as the default status symbol. Local giants like Anta Sports and Li-Ning now build carbon-plated marathon shoes at 20% to 30% lower prices and wrap them in domestic cultural pride. Meanwhile, APLA—spanning Tokyo, Seoul, and Latin America—held steady at $6.23 billion in FY2026, while Converse imploded by more than 30% to $1.17 billion, surviving largely on a single canvas shoe, the Chuck Taylor, and posting an underlying operating loss once you strip out its $21 million tariff recovery.

The punchline of Chapter 2 is simple: Nike's regional operating margins look lush at 19% to 22%, but they have to pay for $4.61 billion of Global Brand Divisions—the LeBron and Kylian Mbappé contracts, the NFL and NBA kit deals, the Beaverton labs—plus $2.02 billion of Corporate overhead. When North America grows modestly and China shrinks by 26%, there is far less regional profit left over to absorb that central bill.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Always check the unallocated corporate and global brand lines before celebrating regional margins; Nike's central athlete-endorsement and R&D bill is a fixed tax on every pair of shoes sold worldwide.

book_subsections.title: Why Product Mix and Jordan Brand Matter for Gross Margin
paragraphs: Before we leave the segment map, look at the product-category split underneath those geographies. Footwear drives roughly 66% of consolidated revenue—more than $30.5 billion in FY2026—while Apparel contributes roughly 28% (~$13.1 billion) and Equipment about 6% (~$2.8 billion). That footwear dominance is a double-edged sword. On the upside, proprietary footwear cushioning platforms like Air, ZoomX, and ReactX command higher engineering barriers to entry than basic cotton-poly fleece apparel. On the downside, footwear carries heavier tooling, mold, and sizing complexity, which means forecasting errors—like overproducing Air Force 1 and Dunk colorways—create far stickier markdown overhangs than apparel.

Embedded inside those numbers is Jordan Brand, a multi-billion-dollar cultural franchise that functions almost like a luxury-streetwear subsidiary within Nike. When Jordan retros are managed with tight scarcity on the SNKRS app and Tier-0 boutiques, they generate some of the highest gross margins in the entire portfolio. When management over-releases Air Jordan 1 mid-top and low-top variants to chase quarterly volume, resale premiums evaporate and full-price sell-through slows across both wholesale and direct channels. Under Elliott Hill's 'Sport Offense', re-anchoring Jordan Brand back to performance basketball and disciplined retro pacing is just as critical to margin recovery as fixing Nike Running.

book_subsections.title: Walking the Floor Across Four Continents: From Chicago to Shanghai
paragraphs: To feel how Nike's $46.4 billion machine actually turns raw foam and fabric into operating profit, you and I need to step inside three different stores on three continents. Start in Chicago, where a marathoner walks into Dick's Sporting Goods or a local run-specialty shop and picks up a $140 to $160 Nike Pegasus 41 or Vomero 18. She is buying dual-density ReactX and ZoomX cushioning engineered in Beaverton's Sport Research Lab. A contract factory in Vietnam—where 52% of Nike's footwear is made—built that pair for roughly $28 to $35 landed cost, shipped it to Nike's Memphis hub, and sold it to Dick's at roughly $75 wholesale. When North America wholesale rebounded 9% in Q1 FY2027 while Nike pruned promotional Classics, full-price replenishment like that Chicago sale anchored North America's $20,511 million FY2026 revenue and 21.5% underlying segment margin—once you strip out the $965 million one-time IEEPA tariff recovery booked in Q4.

Cross the Atlantic to London or Paris, and the competitive temperature rises immediately. A 22-year-old amateur footballer browsing JD Sports or Nike.com for Mercurial cleats or a Paris Saint-Germain match jersey keeps footwear at roughly 61% of EMEA's quarterly revenue—$1,821 million of $2,975 million in Q4 FY2026—with apparel at 33%, or $982 million. On the street outside, though, Adidas's Samba and Gazelle terrace silhouettes alongside On and HOKA have stolen lifestyle and running mindshare, pulling EMEA's FY2026 EBIT down 6% to $2,417 million and Q1 FY2027 revenue down 5% currency-neutral to $3.18 billion. Now fly east to a Shanghai Nike Rise flagship or scroll Tmall, and you see Nike's sharpest pain point: domestic giants Anta Sports, at RMB 80.2 billion or roughly $11.2 billion in 2025 revenue, and Li-Ning now match Nike's carbon-plate running tech at 20% to 30% lower prices, driving Greater China down 11% in FY2026 to $5,855 million and 22% reported—26% currency-neutral—to $1.18 billion in Q1 FY2027.

book_subsections.title: APLA, Converse, and the $6.6 Billion Central Tax
paragraphs: Two smaller pieces complete the geographic and brand puzzle, and both carry important clues for you as an analyst. In Asia Pacific and Latin America, or APLA, a young professional in Tokyo, Seoul, or São Paulo buying an Ava Rover hybrid or Jordan retro apparel through local digital apps helped hold FY2026 revenue virtually flat at $6,234 million, generating $1,387 million in segment EBIT at a 22.2% margin—though foreign-exchange swings and localized pricing tiers clipped EBIT by 9% year-over-year. Converse, by contrast, shows what happens when a brand lacks technical sport depth. Picture a college student buying a $65 Chuck Taylor All Star canvas sneaker at a mall outlet: without performance running or basketball innovation behind it, Converse revenue plunged 31% across FY2025 and FY2026 from $1,692 million to $1,174 million, and fell another 28% in Q1 FY2027 to $263 million, posting an underlying operating loss of $3 million once you remove its $21 million IEEPA tariff recovery.

That brings us back to the biggest trap on Nike's segment page. Regional EBIT margins of 19.2% in EMEA, 21.9% in Greater China, 22.2% in APLA, and 21.5% underlying in North America look extraordinary until you remember the $6,628 million central bill sitting underneath them: $4,605 million in Global Brand Divisions for athlete contracts, league kits, and Beaverton R&D, plus $2,023 million in Corporate overhead. Subtract that fixed central tax, and consolidated FY2026 EBIT margin compresses to 8.3% reported—and roughly 6.2% excluding the $986 million tariff recovery.
